fields.Front: Why do most PySpark applications prefer DataFrames over raw RDDs?
fields.Back: DataFrames carry a schema and run through Spark's Catalyst optimizer and Tungsten execution engine, giving much better performance than RDDs' unoptimized, low-level operations.

fields.Front: What does "lazy evaluation" mean in Spark?
fields.Back: Spark builds up a logical execution plan from transformations but doesn't actually run any computation until an action is called.

fields.Front: Give two examples of Spark transformations.
fields.Back: e.g. filter(), select(), withColumn(), groupBy() — each returns a new DataFrame/RDD lazily, without triggering computation.

fields.Front: Give two examples of Spark actions.
fields.Back: e.g. collect(), count(), show(), write() — these trigger execution of the accumulated transformation plan.
A chunk of a distributed dataset that lives on one node/executor; Spark processes partitions in parallel as its basic unit of parallelism.

What is a "shuffle" in Spark, and why is it expensive?
fields.Back: Redistributing data across partitions/nodes over the network (needed for operations like groupBy, joins, or repartition) — expensive due to network I/O, disk spills, and serialization.

Why use Spark instead of pandas for big data processing?
fields.Back: Spark distributes both data and computation across a cluster of machines, so it can handle datasets far larger than one machine's memory — pandas runs single-node, in-memory only.

repartition(n) does a full shuffle to produce exactly n partitions (can increase or decrease count); coalesce(n) merges existing partitions without a full shuffle, so it's cheaper but can only decrease the count.

fields.Front: If all Spark transformations are lazy, what actually triggers execution?
What does df.cache() (or .persist()) do, and when is it useful?
fields.Back: It materializes the DataFrame/RDD and keeps it in memory (or memory+disk) after the first computation, avoiding recomputation when the same DataFrame is reused across multiple actions.

fields.Front: In Spark SQL, what is the Catalyst optimizer responsible for?
fields.Back: Analyzing and rewriting logical query plans — predicate pushdown, column pruning, join reordering, etc. — into an efficient physical execution plan.
Resilient Distributed Dataset — Spark's low-level, immutable collection of objects partitioned and distributed across a cluster.

fields.Text: Spark builds a {{c1::DAG (directed acyclic graph)}} of stages from a chain of transformations, then schedules {{c2::tasks}} to run that DAG on executors, one task per partition.
